spans.text: What This Guide Covers
This is a practical, step-by-step guide to one specific, legal activity: using the mail-in
"Alternative Method of Entry"

(AMOE) that U.S. sweepstakes casinos are required to offer, to receive free sweepstakes credits without buying anything, and then, if and when you accumulate enough, redeeming those credits and moving the proceeds to your bank account.
It covers three stages:
1. Requesting sweeps credits by mail, correctly, so your entries are not rejected.
2. Tracking what you send and receive so the effort stays organized.
3. Cashing out: how redemption, crypto conversion, and off-ramping to a bank actually work, and where the friction is.
It does not cover playing the casino games, betting strategy, or any method that requires a purchase. The entire point of the mail-in route is that it is free to enter.
What Are Sweepstakes Casinos and Sweeps Cash?
Sweepstakes casinos (Stake.us, Pulsz, Chumba, and others) operate under U.S. sweepstakes law rather than gambling law. They typically use a two-currency system:
A play-only currency (often called Gold Coins) that has no cash value and is just for fun.
A promotional sweepstakes currency (Sweeps Cash, Stake Cash, Sweeps Coins, the name varies) that can, under the platform's rules, be redeemed for prizes or cash once you meet certain conditions.
Because these are sweepstakes and not gambling, the law requires a way to obtain the sweepstakes currency without any purchase. That free path is the mail-in request this book is about.
Check Your State First

The legal ground under sweepstakes casinos is shifting. Beginning in 2025, several states, including California, New York, New Jersey, and Connecticut, passed laws banning online sweepstakes casinos, and other states have bills pending. Platforms respond by closing accounts and refusing new players in those states, and by excluding them in their official rules.
Before you buy a single stamp:
Open the platform's official Sweepstakes Rules and find the list of excluded states.
Confirm your state is not on it, and that you meet the minimum age (usually 18, sometimes 21).
Recheck every few months. A state can be added to the excluded list at any time, and any balance you hold may be affected.

If your state is excluded, stop here. Do not use a different address, a mail forwarding service, or a VPN to get around it. That breaks the rules you agreed to, and platforms void entries and close accounts for it.
Why Companies Offer Free Mail-In Entry

There is nothing secret or exploitative about this. Companies offer the no-purchase mail-in method because they are legally required to. A sweepstakes cannot force a purchase as the only way to enter. Offering the free route is what keeps them classified as a legal sweepstakes rather than illegal gambling.

They can afford it because most users never bother with the mail, most who receive free credits play them back into the games, and the promotional cost counts as ordinary marketing spend. In other words: the free entry is real and legitimate, and you are allowed to use it. Just don't expect the amounts to be large. They are sized as a promotion, not a paycheck.
Realistic Expectations
Here is the honest version, because most guides skip it.

Each valid mail-in request typically yields a small amount of sweeps currency. To turn that into money in your bank, you generally have to: accumulate enough of it, meet the platform's minimum-play and minimum-redemption thresholds, pass identity verification (KYC), and then move the payout through a redemption method (often crypto) and out to your bank, each step with its own fees and delays.

For a patient, organized person who verifies the current rules and keeps at it, mail-in sweepstakes can produce a modest, occasional supplement: the value of some free entertainment credit and a little cash. It is not a salary, it is not passive, and it is not guaranteed. Anyone promising a fixed monthly income from mailing letters is selling a fantasy. Go in with that framing and you will not be disappointed.
What You'll Need
Blank index cards or plain 3×5 request cards (handwriting is required, see Chapter 2).
Standard envelopes and first-class postage.
A pen with legible ink.
A registered, verified account on the platform you're mailing (in your own legal name and address).
A simple log: a notebook or a spreadsheet (Chapter 6).
Optionally, for cashing out: a crypto wallet and an off-ramp method (Chapter 3).
Budget a few dollars a week in cards and postage, and realistic time for handwriting each card. Both count against your net return, so keep them low.

The single most common reason a mail-in entry fails is a formatting or handwriting mistake. Follow the platform's current official rules exactly. The steps below reflect the typical structure of a Stake.us-style request; always confirm the wording, required fields, and address in the platform's current Sweepstakes Rules before mailing.
Step 1: Read the Current Official Rules
Before writing anything, open the platform's official Sweepstakes Rules (on Stake.us this has historically lived in the Terms & Conditions). Note exactly:
The required fields and the exact order they must appear in.
The exact declaration sentence they require you to copy.
Any request code or reference number they ask you to include, and how to obtain it. (Some platforms ask for a specific code; requirements differ and change. Do not assume, verify.)
The current mailing address, which can change at any time.

Tip: Some platforms require a unique request code that you generate inside your account before each mailing. If the rules mention one, get a fresh code for every card. Whatever the current official rules say is what governs your entry.
Step 2: Handwrite the Request Card

A participant must personally handwrite all required information on one side of a single card. Legibility is critical. If the platform decides your handwriting is unreadable, the entry is void, at their sole discretion.
Handwrite the required information in the exact order the current rules specify. For a typical request that means:
Full name, as shown on your government-issued ID.
Your account username.
The return/residential address registered to your account.
The email address registered to your account.
The required request code or reference, if the current rules call for one.
The exact declaration statement the rules require you to include, copied word for word.
Handwriting rules that are almost universal:
Each entry must be handwritten by the participant.
No stencils, copying machines, printed labels, or pre-printed cards.
One request card per envelope.
Missing or unreadable details mean rejection.
A Sample Card Layout

Here is how a typical card is laid out. The bracketed items are placeholders. Replace them with your own details, and use the exact field order and declaration wording from your platform's current rules.
Line What to write
[Full legal name, as on your ID]
Account username]
Street address registered to your account]
City, State, ZIP]
Email address registered to your account]
Request code, only if the rules require one]
Declaration sentence, copied word for word from the rules]

Write slowly, in block capitals if your handwriting is hard to read, and keep a little space between lines. If you make a mistake, start a new card. Crossed-out or corrected cards are a common reason for rejection.
Step 3: Address and Mail the Envelope
Confirm the current mailing address in the official rules, then:
Place only one request card in the envelope.
Handwrite your return address on the front.
Write any label the rules require on the envelope (for example, a
"Sweeps Cash"
or credits label).
Mail from the same state or province as your verified residential address. Entries mailed from a different location, or through commercial sweepstakes-entry services, are typically rejected.
Tip: Mailing addresses for these programs change without notice. Confirm the current address on the platform's official site before every mailing so your card doesn't go to a dead box.
Step 4: Avoid the Common Rejection Mistakes
Illegible handwriting: write neatly; if in doubt, print your letters.
Pre-printed or copied material: everything must be handwritten.
More than one card per envelope: only the rules-permitted number counts.
Mailing from the wrong state: must match your verified address.
Missing or wrong code/declaration: include exactly what the current rules require.
Pre-Mailing Checklist
Run through this before you seal each envelope:
My state is not on the platform's excluded list.
I read the current official rules this week.
Every required field is on the card, in the required order.
The declaration is copied word for word.
The request code (if required) is fresh and written correctly.
Everything is handwritten by me, on one side of one card.
There is exactly one card in the envelope.
